newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Caltex Sri Lanka unit awaits fate of monopoly.
newsitem.headline: Caltex Sri Lanka unit awaits fate of monopoly.

text.p: Sri Lanka might soon end the monopoly enjoyed by Lanka Lubricants Ltd, the local unit of Caltex, but the company is well placed to battle competition, a top company official said on Thursday.

"Lanka Lubricants is now blending international Caltex brands locally and also exporting. The only grey area is whether the government will allow us to retain our monopoly status as the sole producer and distributor of lubricants," Ronald Hopkins, general manager of Lanka Lubricants told Reuters on Thursday.
The government has said it could revoke the monopoly any time after April 1.
A senior government official, who declined to be identified, said it was likely the monopoly would be ended.
"In all likelihood the local lubricant oil market would be opened up for competition," the official told Reuters.
Lanka Lubricants was carved out of the state-owned Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) and floated separately in 1992.
It was privatised in 1994 when the government sold 51 percent of the capital to Caltex, jointly owned by Chevron Corp and Texaco Corp, for $10.2 million.

Hopkins said Lanka Lubricants had already spent 180 million rupees ($3.12 million) on upgrading its blending and packaging facility in the Colombo suburb of Kolonnawa in the past three years. Another 40 million rupees has been earmarked for 1997.

International Caltex brands of engine oils were introduced in late 1996 and a further 20 brands of locally blended Caltex transmission fluids and brake oils among others are due to be introduced in the next two months.
Analysts said the company was strongly placed to overcome competition, which may come from imports once the market is opened up, mostly due to its strong marketing network.
"Due to the huge capital investment needed to blend locally, competitors will be limited to imports," said Channa Kurukulasooriya, head of research at brokerage Lanka Seucrities.
"And since Lanka Lubricants has a contract under which CPC's 1,000 owned and managed outlets can sell only its products, an importer will find it difficult (to break into the market)."
Lanka Lubricants' net profit for the year to December 1996 was 135 million rupees and is forecast to rise to 160 million in 1997, Kurukulasuriya said.
"Growth will come mainly from exports where there is room for volume expansion, and better margins on local sales," he said.
Hopkins said the company expects volume growth of six percent in the local market in 1997, compared to growth of four percent in 1996.
